lead: Glycerin (glycerol) is a colorless, odorless, sweet-tasting, viscous sugar alcohol that mixes freely with water and is hygroscopic, meaning it draws in moisture.[1] It is one of the most common ingredients in skin care, hair care, soaps, shaving products and personal lubricants, where it works as a humectant and gives products a smooth, soft feel.[1][2]

In appearance terms, glycerin's job is hydration. By pulling water into the outer layer of skin it helps skin look and feel plumper and smoother, and dermatology reviews describe it as improving stratum corneum hydration, barrier function and skin mechanical properties.[2] That is why it sits near the top of the ingredient list of many moisturizers, cleansers and after-shave products that people use for a smoother, less flaky complexion.

Wikipedia classifies humectants as water-attracting substances that hold moisture; they are distinguished in skin care from emollients, which soften, and occlusives, which reduce water loss, and glycerin is among the most widely used cosmetic humectants because it is effective and inexpensive [17]. Humectant-rich products have been reported in xerosis studies to improve moisturization without harming the barrier, though some users report stinging [17].

Beyond cosmetics it is widely used in medicine and food: as a laxative in suppositories, as an excipient in tablets and syrups, and as the food additive E422.[1] Bodybuilders also discuss it as a pre-workout and pre-contest additive, because it binds water and is said to increase muscle fullness.[7][8] The Cosmetic Ingredient Review expert panel concluded in 2019 that glycerin is safe as used in cosmetics at current concentrations and practices.[3]

angle.text: Glycerin is a humectant in moisturizers, cleansers, shaving products and hair care. By keeping the outermost skin layer hydrated, it helps skin look smoother and less flaky, and many people use glycerin-containing products for dry or winter-roughened skin. Some bodybuilders also add it to pre-workout drinks or contest-week routines for a fuller look.

paras: Glycerin is used as a humectant and lubricant in skin care, hair care, shaving cream and soaps, and topical glycerin has been used for ichthyosis and xerosis (dry skin).[1] The cosmetic safety assessment lists many labelled functions: denaturant, fragrance ingredient, hair conditioning agent, humectant, oral care agent, skin protectant, skin conditioning agent and viscosity-decreasing agent.[3] It appears on the WHO Essential Medicines List in the context of atopic eczema.[1]

A 2008 review in the British Journal of Dermatology describes glycerol as a normal component of skin as well as a long-standing ingredient of topical preparations. It notes that skin produces and transports glycerol through the aquaporin-3 channel and through fat metabolism in the sebaceous (oil-gland) unit, and that glycerol plays a role in hydration, elasticity and barrier repair.[2]

Rectal glycerin acts as a laxative, oral glycerin has been used to temporarily lower eye pressure in emergencies, and it is used to preserve red blood cells before freezing and to preserve tissue grafts.[1] Glycerin-containing eye drops are sold over the counter for temporary relief of dryness and irritation, and their US labels advise users to stop use and see a doctor if pain, vision changes or redness persist.[9] It is a common solvent in oral and injectable drug formulations.[4] In vaping liquids, vegetable glycerin is a common solvent, and studies have examined the carbonyl compounds produced when it is heated.[5]

Glycerol appears in the Australian Institute of Sport's Group A category of nutritional ergogenic aids and has been included in systematic reviews of supplements for sport.[10] In lifting communities, vegetable glycerin is sometimes added to pre- and intra-workout drinks. One T Nation log describes mixing a gallon of vegetable glycerin into pre-workout and intra-workout drinks and reports one of the best muscle pumps of the poster's life.[7] Another forum member says glycerol added to a pre-workout drink binds water and gives a prolonged pump, and a contest-prep log mentions buying vegetable glycerin for the carb-up the day before a show.[8][11] These are individual reports rather than trial results.

The most detailed overview is the 2008 review, which summarises effects reported in the literature: improved stratum corneum hydration, improved barrier function and mechanical properties, protection against irritating stimuli, faster desmosomal degradation (the natural shedding of surface cells), acceleration of wound healing and an antimicrobial effect.[2] It says glycerol-containing products improve skin properties in conditions marked by dry skin and a weakened barrier, such as atopic dermatitis, and that raising epidermal hydration is relevant to dryness aggravated by cold, dry weather such as winter xerosis.[2]

Comparison studies of moisturizers have looked at glycerin-containing formulations as one type among several. A randomized phase II trial in adults with atopic dermatitis compared different types of emollient cream and reported that they had diverse physiological effects on the skin barrier, indicating that the choice of moisturizer type is not interchangeable.[6]

sections.h: How it works in skin care
paras: Glycerin is a small polyol with several hydroxyl groups that form hydrogen bonds with water, which is why humectants of this kind pull water vapor from the air and from deeper skin layers toward the stratum corneum [17]. Formulators commonly pair it with emollients and occlusives, since humectants alone attract water but do not seal it in [17]. Pyroglutamic acid and urea are other humectants, the former a component of the skin's natural moisturizing factor [17].

The 2008 dermatology review adds that skin itself transports glycerol through aquaporin-3 channels, and that glycerol is part of how the epidermis stays hydrated and repairs its barrier [2]. Wikipedia lists the cosmetic roles of glycerol as lubrication and moisture retention in skin care, hair products, toothpaste, shaving cream and personal lubricants [1].

A 2017 Cochrane review of emollients and moisturisers for eczema covered 77 trials with 6,603 participants. It found that most moisturisers showed some benefit, with lower investigator-assessed severity and fewer flares, that adverse events did not differ significantly from controls, and that glycerol-containing moisturisers improved investigator-assessed SCORAD without meeting the minimal important difference. The authors reported no reliable evidence that one moisturiser outperforms another [19].

These are studies in people with eczema. For people without skin disease who use glycerin products for a smoother or less flaky complexion, the research base is the broader moisturizer and humectant literature described above [2][17][19].

The Cosmetic Ingredient Review expert panel reviewed animal and human data and concluded that glycerin is safe as a cosmetic ingredient in the practices of use and concentration described in its assessment.[3]

Wikipedia reports very low oral toxicity in animal tests, though excessive intake by children, for example through glycerol-containing slush drinks, can cause symptoms such as hypoglycemia, nausea and loss of consciousness; UK and Scottish food authorities issued guidance in 2023.[1] Contamination of glycerol with diethylene glycol has caused deaths in the past, and the FDA advised batch testing in 2007.[1]

Outside skin care, glycerol has been studied in athletes as part of hyperhydration, where it is taken with fluid in the hours before exercise. A 2007 meta-analysis reported that glycerol-induced hyperhydration increased fluid retention by about 7.7 mL per kg of body weight compared with water alone, and endurance performance by about 2.6 percent, but it rested on only four studies and the authors called for more research before firm conclusions about performance [18].

Bodybuilding forums use the same ingredient for a different purpose, the muscle pump and fullness, and those reports are anecdotal [7][8][11]. Athletes' use of supplements is also covered in sports-nutrition reviews that place glycerol in a category of ergogenic aids [10].

Glycerin is inexpensive and widely available because it is a by-product of soap and biodiesel manufacture [1]. Wikipedia lists its use in skin care, hair products, toothpaste and shaving cream [1]. In vaping, vegetable glycerin is a common base liquid, and the carbonyl compounds formed on heating have been studied [5]. In 2023 UK regulators asked slush-drink makers to reduce glycerol levels after children needed treatment, and Food Standards Scotland advises against the drinks for under-sevens [1].

Carl Wilhelm Scheele discovered glycerin as the sweet principle of fat; Michel Eugène Chevreul coined the name glycérine around 1811, and the alcohol-style name glycerol was introduced in 1872.[1] During World War II, synthetic production from propylene was prioritized because glycerol is a precursor to nitroglycerin, and biofuel production since around 2010 has created a surplus.[1] Because it is a by-product of soap making and biodiesel manufacture, it is inexpensive and widely available, which has helped keep it a staple of consumer products.[1]

Several research strands involve glycerol. The 2008 dermatology review and the 2019 safety assessment summarise human and animal data on its effects on skin and its cosmetic safety.[2][3] A randomized phase II trial examined emollient creams in adults with atopic dermatitis and found different emollient types influenced the skin barrier differently.[6] Systematic reviews of sports supplements list glycerol alongside caffeine, creatine and sodium bicarbonate in the ergogenic-aid category.[10]

Registered trials of glycerin itself mostly concern other uses. A 220-infant randomized trial examined prophylactic glycerin suppositories for feeding intolerance in very low birth weight preterm infants, a 16-patient phase 4 trial examined suppositories for bowel function in gastroschisis, and a 79-infant trial examined suppositories to reduce jaundice in premature infants.[12][13][14] A controlled study of a cosmetic active ingredient for mild to moderate atopic dermatitis with 44 participants is registered but does not identify glycerin as the active.[15]

timeline.event: The name glycerol, with the alcohol suffix, is introduced.[1]
More than 100 people die in the US after elixir sulfanilamide contaminated with diethylene glycol, an episode Wikipedia places in glycerol's safety history [1].
FDA advises testing glycerol batches for diethylene glycol contamination.[1]
Meta-analysis of glycerol-induced hyperhydration reports increased fluid retention and a small endurance gain across four studies [18].
A review in the British Journal of Dermatology summarises glycerol's origin and functions in skin.[2]
Cochrane review of 77 trials finds most moisturisers beneficial in eczema, with glycerol-containing products improving investigator-assessed severity [19].
The Cosmetic Ingredient Review panel concludes glycerin is safe as used in cosmetics.[3]
UK and Scottish food authorities issue guidance on glycerol in slush drinks for children.[1]

lore.intro: In strength-training forums, glycerin comes up mainly as a pump and water-retention additive, and occasionally as a laxative; in skin-care discussion it is treated as a background humectant.[7][8][16]

claims.claim: Adding vegetable glycerin to a workout drink gives a bigger, longer muscle pump.
claims.believers: Forum members who add glycerin to pre- and intra-workout drinks describe a prolonged pump and one reports the best leg pump of their training history.[7][8]
claims.experts: Glycerol is listed among nutritional ergogenic aids in sports-nutrition reviews, but the abstracts reviewed here do not report a trial of glycerin for muscle fullness.[10]

claims.claim: Vegetable glycerin before a physique show makes muscles look fuller.
claims.believers: A contest-prep log describes obtaining vegetable glycerine to use with the carb-up the day before a competition.[11]
claims.experts: No published trial in the material reviewed measures its effect on stage appearance.

claims.claim: Glycerin works as a quick over-the-counter laxative.
claims.believers: A member of a training forum describes using glycerin for constipation and asks how often it is safe to repeat.[16]
claims.experts: Rectal glycerin is described as a laxative, and registered trials have tested suppositories in infants.[1][12]

claims.claim: Glycerin pulls water into skin and leaves it smoother.
claims.believers: Skin-care users treat it as a background hydrator in moisturizers and cleansers.
claims.experts: Reviews describe glycerol as improving stratum corneum hydration and barrier function, and Wikipedia describes humectants as attracting water to the stratum corneum [2][17].

claims.claim: Glycerin alone is enough; a moisturizer needs nothing else.
claims.believers: Simple glycerin-and-water formulas are popular with minimalists.
claims.experts: Wikipedia distinguishes humectants from emollients and occlusives, and the Cochrane review found no reliable evidence that one moisturiser is better than another [17][19].

claims.claim: Glycerol hyperhydration helps endurance and fluid retention.
claims.believers: Athletes describe using glycerol to hold more fluid before hot or long sessions.
claims.experts: A 2007 meta-analysis reported about 7.7 mL/kg more fluid retained and about 2.6 percent better endurance across four studies, and called for more research [18].

claims.claim: Glycerin in drinks can be harmful.
claims.believers: Some commenters warn about large amounts.
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports very low oral toxicity in animals, but excess intake by young children from slush drinks has caused hypoglycemia and collapse, and diethylene glycol contamination has caused deaths [1].

name: Glycerin

card.summary: The ubiquitous humectant in moisturizers and cleansers, with long use but no cosmetic trials.
card.note: Evidence for skin effects here is descriptive; diethylene glycol contamination has been a historical safety issue.

quick.overview:
Glycerin is a thick, sweet, water-attracting liquid that appears in most moisturizers, soaps and many hair and shaving products. It is also used as a laxative, drug excipient and food additive.
It is described as a humectant but has no cosmetic trials; the registered trials found study other uses such as suppositories.
quick.mechanism: It is hygroscopic, so it attracts and holds water, which is why it is described as a humectant that softens skin.
quick.risks: Oral toxicity is described as very low, but large amounts can affect children, and past diethylene glycol contamination caused deaths, leading to FDA batch-testing advice in 2007.
